common_name: Four Season Orchid (Golden Orchid, Chinese Ensifolium Cymbidium)

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring and pot into a fast-draining terrestrial orchid mix of fine bark, perlite, and a little charcoal, keeping the grassy foliage in bright shade rather than direct sun.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered shade in a fast-draining terrestrial orchid mix, watering thoroughly and then letting the surface dry slightly before the next soak. Unlike the large winter-blooming standard cymbidiums, Cymbidium ensifolium is prized across East Asia for its slender grassy foliage and small, intensely fragrant green-and-maroon flowers that can appear in several flushes through the warmer months rather than just once in winter. Feed lightly with a balanced orchid fertilizer during active growth and reduce watering somewhat in cooler months, dividing crowded clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Repot back-bulb divisions into a coarse bark-based cymbidium mix in a wide, shallow pot; Cymbidium lowianum needs a distinct cool autumn night drop into the 50s Fahrenheit to reliably set its winter flower spikes.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light with cool nights, especially in autumn, since Cymbidium lowianum will not spike reliably without a seasonal temperature drop. This large Himalayan and Southeast Asian species is one of the principal ancestors of the modern standard cymbidium hybrids sold as potted gift plants, producing long, arching sprays of a dozen or more waxy, apple-green flowers marked with a broad red-brown V on the lip. Water freely while pseudobulbs are actively growing, then let the mix dry more between waterings once flower spikes appear, and repot only every two to three years since cymbidiums bloom best when slightly pot-bound.

planting.note: Mount on a slab or plant in a shallow basket rather than a deep pot, since Cymbidium devonianum's flower spikes emerge low and arch downward, needing room to hang clear of the foliage.

directions: Mount or basket-grow in bright, filtered light, allowing the short, pendant flower spikes to hang freely below the foliage rather than training them upright. Native to the Himalayan foothills of India and Nepal, this compact, lithophytic species carries dense, downward-arching racemes of small, dark maroon-purple flowers with a contrasting pale lip, and is a key parent of the popular miniature cascading cymbidium hybrids grown as hanging houseplants. Water regularly through the growing season and reduce moisture somewhat over winter, keeping the plant in a spot with good air movement to prevent rot on the low-hanging spikes.

planting.note: Give Cymbidium tracyanum a large, heavy pot and a coarse bark mix, since it forms one of the biggest plants in the genus and needs generous root room plus a cool autumn night drop to flower well.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light with plenty of room for the long, strap-like foliage, providing cool nights in autumn to trigger the towering, arching flower spikes. Cymbidium tracyanum, native to the mountains of Myanmar, Thailand, and Yunnan, produces some of the largest flowers in the genus, heavily striped in red-brown over yellow-green with a spicy, musky fragrance that carries well beyond the plant. Water generously while in active growth, ease off once flower spikes emerge in late autumn, and expect this vigorous species to take several years to reach flowering size from a young division.

planting.note: Repot annually into fresh, fine bark-and-sphagnum mix, since Miltoniopsis roezlii is sensitive to stale media and salt buildup and grows best where summer heat stays moderate.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light and cool-to-intermediate temperatures, keeping the fine bark mix evenly moist without ever letting it turn stagnant. Native to the cloud forests of Colombia and Panama, Miltoniopsis roezlii bears flat, crystalline white flowers with a yellow-and-red blotch at the base of the lip, a parent species behind many of the white and bicolor Miltoniopsis hybrids sold today. Flush the pot regularly with plain water to prevent fertilizer salts from browning the soft, pleated leaf tips, and provide steady humidity since this species does not tolerate a dry rest.

planting.note: Pot into fine, fresh bark-and-sphagnum mix and grow on a cool, bright windowsill; Herrenhausen pansy orchid is one of the most widely distributed red-flowered Miltoniopsis hybrids and repeats well under home conditions.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light at cool-to-intermediate temperatures, keeping the fine bark-and-sphagnum mix consistently moist but never waterlogged. Bred in Germany and named for the historic Herrenhausen Gardens in Hannover, this hybrid produces rounded, flat, deep wine-red to magenta flowers with a narrow white picotee edge, among the most reliable and heavily awarded of the darker-colored pansy orchid hybrids. Flush the mix regularly with plain water to avoid salt injury to the sensitive foliage, and expect the pleated leaves to crease visibly as an early warning if watering becomes inconsistent.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring as new growth emerges and mount or pot into a fine bark mix in bright, filtered light; Miltonia regnellii is a warm-growing Brazilian species that tolerates average home temperatures unlike the cooler Miltoniopsis hybrids.

directions: Grow warm and humid in bright, filtered light, keeping the bark medium evenly moist through the growing season and slightly drier in winter. Miltonia regnellii, native to the Atlantic coastal forests of Brazil, bears pale pink-to-white sepals and petals paired with a broad, deeply notched rose-pink lip veined in darker purple, carried in sprays of several fragrant flowers in late summer and fall. Unlike the cool-growing Miltoniopsis pansy orchids it is often confused with, this true Miltonia thrives at ordinary warm room temperatures and does not require a cool winter rest.

planting.note: Pot in a well-draining bark-based mix in bright indirect light; Zygopetalum maculatum benefits from cooler nights in fall and winter to help initiate its fragrant flower spikes.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect to lightly filtered direct light in a coarse, well-drained bark mix kept evenly moist rather than allowed to dry out fully, more like a typical houseplant than many drier-growing epiphytes. Zygopetalum maculatum, native to South America, produces the characteristic Zygopetalum flower form of green sepals and petals heavily blotched in chocolate-brown atop a white lip intricately veined in purple, carried on upright spikes with a strong sweet fragrance. Provide a slightly cooler, drier rest after flowering to encourage strong rebloom the following season, and feed lightly with a balanced fertilizer during active growth.

planting.note: Pot into a well-draining bark mix and provide cooler nights in fall to trigger strong spiking; this vigorous Australian-bred hybrid is one of the most widely sold fragrant Zygopetalum grexes in the nursery trade.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a coarse, well-drained bark mix, keeping it consistently moist through active growth and slightly drier during the post-bloom rest. Bred in Australia, 'Advance Australia' is among the most popular and vigorous Zygopetalum hybrids in cultivation, producing tall spikes of large, boldly striped purple-and-green flowers with an intense, hyacinth-like fragrance that fills a room. It flowers reliably on smaller, younger plants than many of its species parents, making it a good entry point into growing this fragrant, cool-loving orchid group.

planting.note: Pot into a medium bark mix or slatted basket in bright, filtered light; Brassia gireoudiana is a cooler-growing cloud-forest species from Costa Rica and Panama that appreciates good air movement and evenly moist roots.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light in a coarse bark mix, keeping the roots evenly moist and providing good air circulation typical of its cool, humid cloud-forest habitat. Brassia gireoudiana is one of the showiest and most fragrant spider orchids, bearing long, spidery, bright yellow flowers heavily spotted with reddish-brown on branching sprays. As with other Brassia species, the elongated flower form mimics a spider to attract wasp pollinators, and plants bloom most freely when given ample root room and consistent moisture through the growing season.

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot loosely in coarse bark in bright, filtered light; Brassia caudata has an unusually wide natural range from Florida and Mexico south through the Caribbean and much of tropical South America.

directions: Mount or pot loosely in a fast-draining bark mix in bright, filtered light, allowing roots to dry briefly between thorough waterings. Brassia caudata carries slender, yellow-green flowers heavily barred in maroon-brown with dramatically elongated, tapering sepals ending in fine tails, and is one of the most widely distributed Brassia species in the wild. Water and fertilize generously while new growths are developing, then ease off slightly once pseudobulbs mature, and expect the classic spidery blooms to appear on arching spikes in spring or summer.

planting.note: Pot in a fine, fast-draining terrestrial orchid mix with added limestone chips, since Paphiopedilum micranthum grows naturally on limestone cliffs in southern China and Vietnam and prefers a slightly alkaline root zone.

directions: Grow in low to moderate light with no direct sun, in a fine, fast-draining mix amended with limestone chips to mimic its native cliffside habitat, and allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings. Paphiopedilum micranthum is notable for producing a single flower disproportionately large for its small, mottled-leaved rosette, with an enormous, rounded, inflated pouch in shades of pink to white that dwarfs the rest of the bloom. Keep humidity moderate to high, feed lightly at quarter strength with each watering, and avoid overpotting this compact, slow-growing species.

planting.note: Pot in a fine, well-drained terrestrial mix with added limestone in a warm, shaded spot; Paphiopedilum bellatulum is a warm-growing limestone species from Thailand, Myanmar, and southern China that resents overwatering of its short roots.

directions: Grow in low, filtered light in a fine, fast-draining terrestrial mix, watering thoroughly but allowing the mix to dry noticeably before the next soak, since this species is prone to rot if kept too wet. Paphiopedilum bellatulum forms a low rosette of broad, attractively mottled leaves and produces a single, rounded, creamy white to pale yellow flower heavily spotted with maroon-purple, quite unlike the narrower, twisted-petal flowers of many other slipper orchids. Provide warm temperatures year-round, moderate humidity, and light, infrequent feeding to suit its naturally slow growth rate.

planting.note: Pot in a fine, fast-draining terrestrial mix with limestone chips in bright shade; Paphiopedilum niveum grows on limestone outcrops in Thailand and Malaysia and needs sharp drainage around its short, fine root system.

directions: Grow in bright shade with no direct sun, in a fine, sharply drained mix amended with limestone, watering moderately and letting the surface dry slightly between waterings to avoid crown rot. Paphiopedilum niveum bears rounded, pure white flowers finely dusted with tiny purple spots above a low rosette of dark green leaves mottled in gray-green, and it is one of the principal parents behind the many white and pastel complex Paphiopedilum hybrids grown today. Maintain warm temperatures, moderate to high humidity, and light, dilute feeding suited to its naturally slow, compact growth.

planting.note: Pot in a fine, well-drained terrestrial orchid mix in bright shade; Paphiopedilum spicerianum comes from cooler foothill elevations in northeastern India and appreciates a slightly cooler winter than many lowland slipper orchids.

directions: Grow in bright shade in a fine, well-drained terrestrial mix kept evenly moist but never waterlogged, giving plants slightly cooler winter nights than typical for the genus. Paphiopedilum spicerianum has plain, unmottled green leaves and a distinctive flower with a broad white dorsal sepal marked by a single bold, dark maroon-green median stripe, above twisted, downswept petals in muted olive and pink tones. Feed lightly during active growth, avoid direct sun which quickly scorches the foliage, and expect flowering in fall to early winter on well-established plants.

planting.note: Pot in coarse, fast-draining bark mix in bright, filtered light; Oncidium tigrinum grows at moderate elevations in Mexico and prefers cool-to-intermediate temperatures with a distinct cooler, drier winter rest.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light with cool-to-intermediate temperatures, watering generously while new growths develop and reducing moisture markedly once pseudobulbs mature to trigger flowering. Oncidium tigrinum produces tall, branching sprays of large, bright yellow flowers boldly barred in reddish-brown, with a light, pleasant fragrance, and is a parent of many popular Oncidium-alliance hybrids bred for vigor and easy flowering. Provide a distinct cooler, drier rest in winter to encourage strong spiking, then resume regular watering and feeding as new growth emerges in spring.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark in bright, indirect light; Oncidium 'Wildcat' is a vigorous, easy-flowering hybrid available in several award-winning clones widely sold at garden centers.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark in bright, indirect light, watering when the mix approaches dryness and feeding lightly during active growth. This popular hybrid produces branching sprays of numerous flowers in warm mahogany-brown and gold tones with a mottled, tiger-striped pattern, blooming freely and repeatedly under ordinary windowsill conditions with far less fuss than many of its species parents. Its compact growth and reliable flowering across several named clones have made it one of the more widely distributed Oncidium-alliance hybrids in the retail orchid trade.

planting.note: Pot in a fine, moisture-retentive terrestrial mix and keep constantly damp, never dry; Phragmipedium besseae grows along stream banks and seepage areas in Peru and Ecuador and, unlike most slipper orchids, should never be allowed to dry out.

directions: Keep the fine, moisture-retentive mix constantly damp to wet, standing the pot in a saucer of water if needed, since Phragmipedium besseae grows naturally along Andean stream banks and does not tolerate drying out between waterings the way most slipper orchids do. Discovered in Peru in 1981, this species caused a sensation in the orchid world for its brilliant scarlet-orange to red flowers, a color previously unknown among Paphiopedilum and Phragmipedium slipper orchids, and it has since been used extensively in breeding vividly colored hybrids. Provide bright, filtered light, feed lightly and frequently at low concentration, and use rainwater or low-mineral water where possible since this species is sensitive to salt buildup.

planting.note: Pot in a moisture-retentive terrestrial mix in a tall or hanging container to accommodate the extremely long, trailing petals; Phragmipedium caudatum needs consistently damp roots and cool-to-intermediate mountain temperatures.

directions: Grow in a tall pot or elevated position that allows the flower's extraordinary trailing petals room to hang, keeping the moisture-retentive mix consistently damp and never fully dry. Phragmipedium caudatum, native to cloud forests of the Andes from Peru to Colombia, produces some of the most remarkable flowers in the orchid family, with narrow, ribbon-like petals that continue elongating for days after opening, sometimes reaching two to three feet in length. Provide bright, filtered light and cool-to-intermediate temperatures, and expect each individual flower to remain attractive and slowly lengthening for several weeks.

planting.note: Pot in a fine, moisture-retentive, well-aerated terrestrial mix and grow cool with constant humidity; Phragmipedium kovachii comes from high-elevation cloud forest in northern Peru and resents both drying out and stagnant, waterlogged roots.

directions: Grow cool, in bright filtered light, keeping the fine, well-aerated mix constantly moist and providing high ambient humidity to mimic its native high-elevation cloud forest. First described in 2002 and an immediate sensation among orchid collectors, Phragmipedium kovachii produces the largest flowers in the genus, a stunning magenta-purple, several times the size of related species, on plants that were nearly collected to extinction in the wild before commercial tissue-cultured stock became available. Feed lightly and frequently at low concentration, avoid mineral-heavy water, and expect this slower-growing species to take a few years to reach flowering size.

planting.note: Pot in a moisture-retentive terrestrial mix and keep constantly damp; 'Grande', a cross of Phragmipedium longifolium and Phragmipedium caudatum, is one of the oldest and most widely grown Phragmipedium hybrids and a good introduction to the genus.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light in a moisture-retentive terrestrial mix kept constantly damp, standing the pot in a shallow saucer of water if needed. First registered in the nineteenth century, 'Grande' combines the long, twisting, ribbon-like petals of Phragmipedium caudatum with the more compact, sequential-flowering habit of Phragmipedium longifolium, producing successive blooms in soft green and copper tones over an extended season rather than all at once. Its relative vigor and tolerance of intermediate home temperatures have made it one of the most commonly offered Phragmipedium hybrids for growers new to the genus.
